interviewQuestions.question: How does SignalR decide which transport to use?
interviewQuestions.answer: It negotiates with the client and prefers WebSockets when both the browser and any intermediate proxies support it, falling back to Server-Sent Events or long polling otherwise, without the application needing to choose a transport explicitly.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is a backplane needed when scaling SignalR horizontally?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each server instance only knows about the connections it holds directly; a backplane like Redis relays messages between instances so a broadcast reaches clients connected anywhere, not just on the server that triggered it.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a SignalR group used for?
interviewQuestions.answer: It lets the server send a message to a named subset of connections—for example everyone viewing one order—without tracking connection IDs manually in application code.

note: SignalR handles the transport and connection lifecycle; your application still owns deciding who should receive which message.
tip: Send small, specific payloads over the hub and let the client fetch full detail through a normal API call if needed, rather than pushing large objects.
warning: A dropped connection does not guarantee the client missed nothing or everything; design reconnect logic to reconcile state rather than assume.
latestNote: New guide on hubs, groups, and scaling with a backplane

name: Resilience & Rate Limiting
shortDescription: Protect a service and its callers from cascading failure with retries, circuit breakers, timeouts, and rate limits.
overview: Resilience policies decide how a call behaves when something downstream is slow or failing; rate limiting decides how much load a service accepts in the first place.
detail: Polly composes retry, circuit breaker, timeout, and bulkhead policies around outbound calls so transient failures are absorbed without hammering a struggling dependency. ASP.NET Core's built-in rate limiter protects the service itself from being overwhelmed, using algorithms such as fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, or concurrency limits.

concepts.title: Retry with backoff
concepts.description: Retrying a transient failure after an increasing delay, ideally with jitter, avoids hammering a struggling dependency at a fixed interval.

concepts.title: Circuit breaker
concepts.description: After enough failures, a circuit breaker stops sending calls for a cooldown period, giving a struggling dependency room to recover.

concepts.title: Timeouts and bulkheads
concepts.description: Timeouts stop a call from waiting indefinitely; bulkheads cap concurrent calls to one dependency so it cannot exhaust shared resources.

concepts.title: Rate limiting algorithms
concepts.description: Fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, and concurrency limiters trade off burst tolerance, fairness, and memory cost differently.

architecture.description: Outbound calls pass through composed resilience policies before reaching a dependency, while inbound requests pass through a rate limiter before reaching application code.

code.label: ResilientClient.cs
code.introduction: A named HttpClient gets a standard resilience pipeline once, so every call through it is protected consistently.

bestPractices: Only retry operations known to be safe to repeat, or make them idempotent first.
Add jitter to retry backoff so many clients retrying together don't synchronize into a new spike.
Return a clear 429 response with a Retry-After header when rate limiting a client, instead of silently dropping the request.
Tune circuit breaker thresholds using real failure data, not guessed defaults, and monitor when it opens.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can naive retries make an outage worse?
interviewQuestions.answer: If every client retries immediately and at the same interval after a failure, the retries can synchronize into a load spike that keeps overwhelming the struggling dependency—jittered backoff and circuit breakers exist specifically to prevent this.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a circuit breaker and a retry policy?
interviewQuestions.answer: A retry policy repeats a single call after failure; a circuit breaker tracks failures over time and, once a threshold is crossed, stops sending calls entirely for a cooldown period so a struggling dependency gets room to recover.

interviewQuestions.question: Why rate limit your own API instead of just scaling it?
interviewQuestions.answer: Scaling has limits and cost; rate limiting protects shared resources like a database or downstream dependency from being overwhelmed by a burst, and gives predictable, fair behavior under load instead of an uncontrolled failure.

note: Resilience policies manage how you call others; rate limiting manages how others call you—most production APIs need both.
tip: Test resilience policies by actually injecting failures and latency in a lower environment, not just by reading the configuration.
warning: Stacking retries at multiple layers—client, gateway, and service—without coordination can multiply load on a struggling dependency instead of protecting it.
latestNote: New guide on Polly policies and ASP.NET Core rate limiting

name: Structured Logging
shortDescription: Emit machine-queryable log events with consistent fields instead of formatted strings that are hard to search.
overview: Structured logging captures each log event as a set of named fields rather than a formatted sentence, making logs searchable, filterable, and aggregable at production scale.
detail: Serilog and similar libraries let you write a log message template with named properties; each property is captured as structured data alongside the rendered text. Enrichers attach context such as a correlation ID or environment to every event, and sinks route events to one or more destinations—console, file, or a centralized platform.

concepts.title: Message templates
concepts.description: A log call captures named properties as structured data, not just an interpolated string, so fields remain queryable after the fact.

concepts.title: Enrichers
concepts.description: Enrichers attach consistent context—correlation ID, environment, version—to every log event without repeating it at each call site.

concepts.title: Log levels
concepts.description: Verbose, Debug, Information, Warning, Error, and Fatal levels let you control noise and route events differently by severity.

concepts.title: Sinks
concepts.description: A sink defines where events go—console, file, or a centralized log platform—and multiple sinks can run at once with different filters.

architecture.description: A log call captures structured properties, enrichers attach shared context, and the pipeline writes the enriched event to one or more sinks.

code.label: LoggingSetup.cs
code.introduction: Structured properties in the message template stay queryable; the enricher attaches a correlation ID to every event automatically.
code.code:
Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .Enrich.WithCorrelationId()
    .Enrich.FromLogContext()
    .WriteTo.Console(new CompactJsonFormatter())
    .CreateLogger();

logger.LogInformation(
    "Order {OrderId} placed for {CustomerId} with total {Total}",
    order.Id, order.CustomerId, order.Total);

bestPractices: Log named properties through the message template, not string interpolation, so fields stay structured and queryable.
Attach a correlation ID to every request early and flow it through logs, traces, and outbound calls.
Set log levels deliberately per environment; verbose logging in production is expensive and can leak sensitive detail.
Never log secrets, tokens, or full payloads containing personal data; redact or omit them explicitly.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between structured logging and just writing formatted strings to a file?
interviewQuestions.answer: Structured logging captures each log call's properties as separate, typed fields alongside the message, so a log platform can filter, aggregate, and query on those fields directly instead of parsing free-text strings.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use a message template with named placeholders instead of string interpolation?
interviewQuestions.answer: Named placeholders preserve each value as a distinct property in the structured event; string interpolation collapses everything into one opaque string before logging, losing that structure.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a correlation ID and why does it matter across services?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is an identifier generated at the start of a request and passed through every downstream call and log line, letting you find every log event related to one logical operation across multiple services.

note: Logs are a queryable data source, not just text for a human to scroll through during an incident.
tip: Log at the boundary of a meaningful business event—order placed, payment failed—rather than logging every internal method call.
warning: Logging full request or response bodies by default is a common way secrets and personal data end up in a log platform.
latestNote: New guide on message templates, enrichers, and sinks

name: Semantic Kernel
shortDescription: Microsoft's SDK for building AI-powered .NET applications using LLMs, plugins, memory, and orchestrated agents.
overview: Semantic Kernel is an open-source SDK from Microsoft that lets .NET developers integrate large language models into applications using familiar C# patterns.
detail: Semantic Kernel acts as an orchestration layer between your application and AI services like OpenAI or Azure OpenAI. You define plugins—functions the AI can call—and a kernel routes user intent to the right combination of those plugins. Memory connectors let the AI retrieve relevant context from vector stores, and agents can plan and execute multi-step tasks autonomously.

concepts.title: Kernel and services
concepts.description: The Kernel is the central object that wires together AI services, plugins, and memory, and routes requests through them.

concepts.title: Plugins
concepts.description: C# methods decorated with attributes become tools the LLM can call to read data, call APIs, or trigger business logic.

concepts.title: Memory and embeddings
concepts.description: Text is converted to vector embeddings and stored so the AI can retrieve semantically relevant context before responding.

concepts.title: Agents and planners
concepts.description: Agents reason over a goal and decide which plugins to call and in what order, enabling multi-step autonomous workflows.

architecture.description: A user prompt enters the Kernel, which enriches it with memory context and routes it to the LLM; the model calls plugins as needed before returning a grounded response.

code.label: OrderAssistant.cs
code.introduction: A plugin exposes a C# method as a tool the LLM can call; the kernel wires everything together in one place.

bestPractices: Keep plugins small and focused on one capability so the LLM can choose them reliably.
Store secrets like API keys in Azure Key Vault or environment variables, never in code.
Add memory and retrieval-augmented generation before building agents, as grounded context reduces hallucinations.
Log token usage and latency per kernel invocation so AI costs and performance are visible from the start.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a Semantic Kernel plugin and a prompt template?
interviewQuestions.answer: A plugin is a C# method the LLM can call to perform an action or retrieve data; a prompt template is a structured string passed to the model to guide its text response. Plugins add capabilities; prompt templates shape the conversation.

interviewQuestions.question: What problem does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: LLMs have a fixed training cutoff and no access to private data. RAG retrieves relevant documents from a vector store and injects them into the prompt, grounding the model's response in current, application-specific facts.

interviewQuestions.question: When would you use an agent instead of a single prompt?
interviewQuestions.answer: When the task requires multiple steps, decisions, or tool calls that cannot be predicted upfront—for example, researching a topic and then drafting a summary—an agent can plan and iterate rather than a single prompt producing one fixed response.

note: Semantic Kernel is the orchestration layer, not the model itself. The quality of your plugins and prompts determines how useful the AI actually is.
tip: Start with a single plugin and one well-scoped prompt before adding planners or agents; simpler pipelines are easier to debug and cheaper to run.
warning: Never trust LLM-generated content to drive destructive operations without a human confirmation step or a strict validation layer.
latestNote: New guide on Kernel setup, plugins, and retrieval-augmented generation

name: Domain-Driven Design
shortDescription: Model complex business domains using a shared language, bounded contexts, aggregates, and value objects.
overview: Domain-Driven Design is an approach to software development that puts the business domain at the centre, using a shared language between developers and domain experts to build models that reflect real-world rules.
detail: DDD separates complex business logic into bounded contexts, each with its own model and language. Inside a context, aggregates enforce invariants and act as consistency boundaries; value objects describe domain concepts without identity; domain events capture meaningful things that happened; and repositories provide access to aggregates without leaking persistence details.

concepts.title: Ubiquitous language
concepts.description: A shared vocabulary used by both developers and domain experts in code, tests, and conversations, so the model and the business stay aligned.

concepts.title: Bounded context
concepts.description: An explicit boundary within which a particular domain model and its language are consistent; different contexts can have different models for the same concept.

concepts.title: Aggregates and entities
concepts.description: An aggregate is a cluster of objects treated as one unit for data changes; the root entity controls access and enforces all invariants.

concepts.title: Value objects and domain events
concepts.description: Value objects model concepts by their attributes rather than identity; domain events record meaningful state changes that other parts of the system can react to.

architecture.description: Bounded contexts own their models and communicate through well-defined contracts or domain events, keeping each context independently evolvable.

code.label: Order.cs
code.introduction: An aggregate root enforces its own invariants and raises domain events instead of letting callers mutate state directly.

bestPractices: Involve domain experts when naming concepts; code that uses business language is easier to validate and maintain.
Keep aggregates small—an aggregate that owns too much becomes a bottleneck and a source of contention.
Model domain events in past tense to describe what happened, not what should happen.
Map bounded context relationships explicitly using context maps so cross-boundary dependencies are visible and intentional.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an entity and a value object?
interviewQuestions.answer: An entity has a unique identity that persists over time regardless of attribute changes; a value object is defined entirely by its attributes and has no meaningful identity of its own, so two value objects with the same attributes are interchangeable.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should an aggregate be kept small?
interviewQuestions.answer: Aggregates are loaded and saved as a unit and act as a consistency boundary. A large aggregate increases lock contention, load time, and the risk of unrelated operations blocking each other.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a bounded context and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answer: A bounded context is an explicit boundary within which a domain model is internally consistent. It matters because the same word—like 'customer'—can mean different things in different parts of a business, and mixing those meanings in one model creates confusion and fragile code.

note: DDD is a design philosophy, not a set of mandatory patterns. Apply aggregates and events where the domain is genuinely complex; simpler areas often need only basic CRUD.
tip: Start with a context map and a glossary before writing any code—shared language problems surface quickly and are cheap to fix on paper.
warning: Avoid anemic domain models where aggregates are just data bags and all logic lives in services; this defeats the purpose of encapsulating business rules in the domain.
latestNote: New guide on aggregates, value objects, and bounded contexts

name: Vertical Slice Architecture
shortDescription: Organise code by feature instead of by layer, keeping everything a feature needs together and coupling to a minimum.
overview: Vertical Slice Architecture organises an application around features rather than technical layers, so each feature contains its own endpoint, handler, validation, and data access in one place.
detail: Instead of grouping all controllers together, all repositories together, and all services together, Vertical Slice Architecture puts everything a single use case needs into one folder or file. Changes to one feature touch only that slice, reducing the risk of breaking unrelated features. MediatR is a common companion because it lets each slice define its own command or query and handler without a shared service class.

concepts.title: Feature folders
concepts.description: All code for one feature—endpoint, handler, validator, response type—lives in one folder, making the feature easy to find, change, and delete.

concepts.title: Minimal coupling between slices
concepts.description: Slices share as little as possible. Common infrastructure like database access is shared, but business logic stays inside the slice that owns it.

concepts.title: Each slice owns its contract
concepts.description: A slice defines the request and response types it needs, rather than reusing shared DTOs that accumulate properties for many callers.

concepts.title: Contrast with layered architecture
concepts.description: Layers separate concerns horizontally across the whole application; vertical slices separate concerns vertically per feature, favouring cohesion over uniform abstraction.

architecture.description: Each feature is a self-contained vertical slice from HTTP endpoint to data access; shared infrastructure sits below all slices but no slice depends on another.

code.label: PlaceOrder/
code.introduction: A single file contains the endpoint, command, handler, and response for the Place Order feature—nothing is shared with other features unless it truly belongs to shared infrastructure.

bestPractices: Co-locate the endpoint, handler, validator, and response type in a single file or folder per feature.
Share only what is genuinely shared—database context, auth helpers, base types—not business logic.
Let each slice define the exact request and response shape it needs instead of inheriting a bloated shared DTO.
Use integration tests per slice to verify the full path from HTTP to database without shared test setup getting in the way.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the main advantage of Vertical Slice Architecture over a traditional layered approach?
interviewQuestions.answer: Changes to one feature touch only that slice, reducing the risk of breaking unrelated features and making it easier to reason about what a change affects. Layered architectures spread one feature across many layers, so a change ripples horizontally.

interviewQuestions.question: Does Vertical Slice Architecture replace Clean Architecture?
interviewQuestions.answer: Not necessarily—they answer different questions. Clean Architecture defines where dependencies point; Vertical Slice Architecture defines how to organise code within a project. You can use feature folders inside a clean architecture structure.

interviewQuestions.question: When is Vertical Slice Architecture a poor fit?
interviewQuestions.answer: When features share significant business logic or domain rules that would be duplicated across slices, a richer shared domain model may be a better fit than pure vertical isolation.

note: Vertical Slice Architecture is a code organisation strategy, not a silver bullet. The right amount of sharing between slices depends on how much the features genuinely overlap.
tip: Start by grouping existing files into feature folders without changing any logic—the structure alone usually reveals unexpected coupling.
warning: Taken too far, every slice becoming a copy-paste of the last leads to the same duplication problems that layers were meant to solve; shared infrastructure must still be shared.
latestNote: New guide on feature folders, minimal coupling, and slice-per-feature organisation

name: Microsoft.Extensions.AI
shortDescription: Provider-neutral abstractions and middleware for adding generative AI capabilities to .NET applications.
overview: Microsoft.Extensions.AI provides common .NET abstractions for generative AI services so application code can work with chat, embeddings, and related capabilities without being coupled to one provider SDK.
detail: The abstractions package defines exchange types such as IChatClient and IEmbeddingGenerator, while the higher-level Microsoft.Extensions.AI package adds composable middleware for function invocation, telemetry, caching, and other cross-cutting behavior. Providers implement the interfaces, and applications consume them through dependency injection, which makes provider changes and test doubles much easier to manage.

concepts.title: IChatClient
concepts.description: A common contract for complete and streaming chat responses, messages, tools, and multi-modal content across compatible providers.

concepts.title: IEmbeddingGenerator
concepts.description: A generic abstraction for turning text or other inputs into vector embeddings used by semantic search and retrieval workflows.

concepts.title: Composable middleware
concepts.description: Chat clients can be wrapped with function invocation, caching, telemetry, rate limiting, or custom delegating behavior.

concepts.title: Provider portability
concepts.description: Application services depend on shared abstractions while provider-specific registration remains at the composition root.

architecture.description: Application code calls shared AI abstractions, a middleware pipeline applies cross-cutting behavior, and a provider adapter communicates with the selected model service.

code.label: SupportAssistant.cs
code.introduction: The application service depends only on IChatClient, so provider setup and middleware remain outside the business workflow.

bestPractices: Keep provider-specific construction at the composition root and inject the shared abstractions into application services.
Add telemetry around latency, token use, model identity, and failures without recording sensitive prompt content by default.
Use explicit timeouts, cancellation, retry limits, and rate limits because model calls are remote and comparatively expensive.
Test AI workflows with deterministic fake IChatClient implementations before relying on slower provider integration tests.

interviewQuestions.question: How is Microsoft.Extensions.AI different from Semantic Kernel?
interviewQuestions.answer: Microsoft.Extensions.AI supplies provider-neutral primitives and composable client middleware. Semantic Kernel is a broader orchestration SDK for plugins, agents, prompts, and multi-step AI workflows; the two can be used together.

interviewQuestions.question: Why inject IChatClient instead of a provider SDK client?
interviewQuestions.answer: It keeps application code portable, simplifies tests, and centralizes provider-specific authentication, model selection, and middleware in the composition root.

interviewQuestions.question: What belongs in an AI client middleware pipeline?
interviewQuestions.answer: Cross-cutting concerns such as telemetry, caching, function invocation, rate limiting, safety checks, and resilience belong there when their ordering and failure behavior are explicit.

note: Provider neutrality reduces coupling, but models still differ in supported modalities, tool behavior, context limits, and response quality.
tip: Define one application-level AI use case behind IChatClient first, then add provider selection and middleware only where the use case requires them.
warning: Do not treat provider portability as output equivalence; validate safety, quality, latency, and cost again whenever the model or provider changes.
latestNote: New guide on provider-neutral AI abstractions and middleware

name: .NET MAUI
shortDescription: Build native Android, iOS, macOS, and Windows applications from a shared C# and XAML codebase.
overview: .NET Multi-platform App UI (.NET MAUI) is the .NET framework for creating native mobile and desktop applications with C# and XAML from a shared project.
detail: .NET MAUI provides a single project system, shared controls and layouts, data binding, handlers, app lifecycle APIs, and access to native device capabilities. Shared code targets Android, iOS, macOS through Mac Catalyst, and Windows through WinUI 3. Teams can build native XAML interfaces or host reusable Razor components locally through BlazorWebView, combining web UI reuse with native device access and store packaging.

concepts.title: Single project
concepts.description: One SDK-style project shares code, fonts, images, app metadata, and resources while multi-targeting native platforms.

concepts.title: Handlers
concepts.description: Cross-platform controls map through handlers to native platform views and can be customized globally or per control.

concepts.title: Native and hybrid UI
concepts.description: Use XAML and native controls, or host Razor components locally with BlazorWebView and share them with a Blazor web application through a Razor class library.

concepts.title: Platform integration
concepts.description: Cross-platform APIs cover sensors, connectivity, secure storage, files, and permissions, with direct native APIs available when required.

architecture.description: Shared C# uses native XAML controls or locally hosted Razor components, while MAUI handlers and device services connect the application to each operating system.

code.label: MainPage.xaml.cs
code.introduction: A shared page can call a cross-platform device API while permission and platform details stay behind .NET MAUI abstractions.

bestPractices: Keep business logic and application state in platform-neutral services and view models so they can be unit tested without a device.
Place reusable Razor components in a Razor class library when a Blazor Hybrid app and a Blazor Web App share UI, while isolating host-specific services behind interfaces.
Use handlers or platform folders for genuine native differences instead of scattering platform checks throughout shared code.
Profile startup, memory, rendering, and package size on release builds because debug and emulator behavior can be misleading.

interviewQuestions.question: Does .NET MAUI render one identical UI on every platform?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Shared MAUI controls are mapped to native platform controls through handlers, so behavior and appearance can retain platform conventions while sharing most UI code.

interviewQuestions.question: How does Blazor Hybrid differ from a hosted web app?
interviewQuestions.answer: Blazor Hybrid renders Razor components in a BlazorWebView inside the native MAUI app, with UI assets packaged locally and direct access to .NET and device services; it does not require a browser-hosted WebAssembly application.

interviewQuestions.question: Why must iOS and macOS builds use a Mac?
interviewQuestions.answer: Apple's native toolchain and signing infrastructure are required to compile and package those applications, even when development begins from another operating system.

note: A shared codebase does not remove platform differences; it gives teams one place to share common UI and logic while making native exceptions explicit.
tip: Start with one representative workflow and validate it on physical devices before committing an entire product to a cross-platform UI strategy.
warning: Do not judge production performance from debug builds or emulators alone; measure signed release builds on the oldest supported devices.
latestNote: Blazor Hybrid and shared Razor component guidance added

name: Modular Monolith
shortDescription: Keep one deployable application while enforcing business-module boundaries that can evolve independently.
overview: A modular monolith is a single deployable application divided into strongly encapsulated business modules with explicit contracts and controlled dependencies.
detail: Unlike a traditional monolith organized mainly by technical layers, a modular monolith groups code and data ownership around business capabilities. Modules communicate through public contracts or in-process messages, hide their internal models, and can own separate schemas while still sharing one process and deployment pipeline. It preserves operational simplicity and leaves room to extract a module only when independent scaling or deployment provides proven value.

concepts.title: Business modules
concepts.description: Each module owns a cohesive capability, its application behavior, domain model, persistence, and public contract.

concepts.title: Enforced boundaries
concepts.description: Internal types stay inaccessible and dependency rules prevent modules from reaching into one another's implementation details.

concepts.title: Module communication
concepts.description: Public interfaces, commands, queries, or events make cross-module interactions explicit and replace direct table or class access.

concepts.title: Single deployment
concepts.description: Modules compile and run together, avoiding distributed transactions and network failure while retaining architectural separation.

architecture.description: One host composes independently owned modules; modules communicate through contracts while sharing the process and, when appropriate, a database server with isolated schemas.

code.label: OrdersModule.cs
code.introduction: A module exposes only registration and endpoint mapping while keeping handlers, entities, and persistence types internal.

bestPractices: Define modules from business capabilities and bounded contexts, not arbitrary folders or deployment aspirations.
Make module internals inaccessible and enforce dependency rules with architecture tests in continuous integration.
Give each module ownership of its tables or schema; cross-module reads should use contracts or deliberately maintained read models.
Extract a module into a service only when independent deployment, scaling, ownership, or isolation justifies the distributed-system cost.

interviewQuestions.question: How does a modular monolith differ from a layered monolith?
interviewQuestions.answer: A layered monolith groups code by technical role across the system, while a modular monolith groups cohesive business capabilities and restricts dependencies across those module boundaries.

interviewQuestions.question: What advantages does it have over microservices?
interviewQuestions.answer: It keeps calls and transactions in process, simplifies deployment and debugging, and avoids network and consistency complexity while still making business boundaries explicit.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you stop module boundaries from eroding?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use internal visibility, small public contracts, separate schemas or contexts, architecture tests, and code ownership rules that fail builds when forbidden dependencies appear.

note: The value comes from enforced modularity, not from putting the word Modules in a folder name.
tip: Start with the business capability that changes most often and define its public contract before reorganizing the rest of the application.
warning: A shared database becomes hidden coupling when modules query or update one another's tables directly.
latestNote: New guide on module boundaries and monolith-to-services tradeoffs

name: Source Generators
shortDescription: Generate strongly typed C# during compilation to remove repetitive runtime work and boilerplate.
overview: C# source generators are Roslyn compiler components that inspect compilation inputs and add new source code to the same compilation.
detail: Generators are useful when a library can discover declarations or configuration at build time and emit strongly typed code instead of relying on runtime reflection or handwritten repetition. Incremental generators model the work as cached transformations, allowing the compiler to rerun only the affected steps as source changes. Generated output is additive: a generator can create new code but cannot rewrite the user's existing syntax tree.

concepts.title: Compiler integration
concepts.description: A generator receives compilation-related inputs and contributes generated syntax trees before the final assembly is emitted.

concepts.title: Incremental pipeline
concepts.description: IIncrementalGenerator builds cacheable, composable transformations so unchanged inputs do not repeat expensive work.

concepts.title: Candidate filtering
concepts.description: Syntax providers first select inexpensive candidates, then semantic analysis confirms symbols and attributes that matter.

concepts.title: Generated contracts
concepts.description: Consumers see normal strongly typed C# with compile-time diagnostics, navigation, and no runtime code-emission requirement.

architecture.description: The compiler feeds syntax and semantic inputs through an incremental pipeline, which emits generated C# that joins user code in the final compilation.

code.label: BuildInfoGenerator.cs
code.introduction: A minimal incremental generator contributes a strongly typed build-information class during compilation.

bestPractices: Prefer IIncrementalGenerator for new generators and keep each transformation deterministic and free of mutable shared state.
Filter syntax cheaply before requesting semantic models, and combine only the inputs required to produce an output.
Generate readable, stable source with unique hint names so developers can inspect and debug the result.
Report diagnostics for invalid user input instead of throwing exceptions or silently generating incomplete code.

interviewQuestions.question: When does a source generator run?
interviewQuestions.answer: It runs as part of compilation and contributes source before the compiler emits the final assembly; it is not a runtime code-generation mechanism.

interviewQuestions.question: Why prefer an incremental generator?
interviewQuestions.answer: Its pipeline lets Roslyn cache intermediate results and rerun only work affected by changed inputs, improving IDE and build performance.

interviewQuestions.question: Can a source generator modify existing source code?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Generators add new source files to a compilation. Analyzers and code fixes can diagnose or offer edits to user code, but generation itself is additive.

note: Source generators and analyzers share Roslyn infrastructure but solve different problems: generators add code, while analyzers report diagnostics.
tip: Ship snapshot tests for generated source and compilation tests for diagnostics so formatting and API contracts remain stable.
warning: A generator that scans every syntax node or performs file and network I/O can make typing and builds noticeably slower.
latestNote: New guide on Roslyn incremental compile-time generation

name: ML.NET
shortDescription: Train and consume classical machine-learning models for classification, regression, recommendation, forecasting, and more in .NET.
overview: ML.NET is an open-source, cross-platform machine-learning framework for training custom models and running predictions inside .NET applications.
detail: ML.NET expresses data preparation and algorithms as a pipeline that is fitted to training data to produce an immutable model. It supports tasks including binary and multiclass classification, regression, clustering, recommendation, anomaly detection, forecasting, and integrations for selected deep-learning scenarios. Models can be trained code-first or with tooling, saved as artifacts, and loaded into applications for local inference.

concepts.title: MLContext
concepts.description: The entry point for loading data, defining pipelines, training models, evaluating results, and saving artifacts.

concepts.title: IDataView
concepts.description: A lazy, schema-aware representation that lets ML.NET process datasets larger than memory through composable transforms.

concepts.title: Estimator pipeline
concepts.description: Data transforms and a trainer are chained, then Fit learns parameters and produces an immutable transformer model.

concepts.title: Evaluation and inference
concepts.description: Task-specific metrics validate a held-out dataset before the saved model is loaded for predictions in an application.

architecture.description: Training data passes through preparation and a trainer to create a versioned model artifact, which an application loads to perform local predictions.

code.label: SentimentModel.cs
code.introduction: A text-featurization and binary-classification pipeline trains a small sentiment model and uses it for a local prediction.

bestPractices: Split training, validation, and test data before experimentation to avoid evaluating a model on examples it learned from.
Choose metrics that match the business cost of false positives and false negatives instead of optimizing accuracy alone.
Version the model together with its input schema, feature pipeline, training data lineage, and evaluation results.
Monitor production data and predictions for drift, and retrain only through a repeatable, reviewed pipeline.

interviewQuestions.question: How is ML.NET different from generative AI libraries?
interviewQuestions.answer: ML.NET primarily trains and runs task-specific predictive models such as classifiers and regressors, while generative AI libraries integrate foundation models that create or transform content.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an estimator and a transformer?
interviewQuestions.answer: An estimator describes a learnable pipeline stage. Calling Fit on data produces a transformer containing the learned parameters that can transform new data.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is a held-out test set important?
interviewQuestions.answer: It estimates how the trained model generalizes to unseen data; evaluating on training examples produces overly optimistic metrics and hides overfitting.

note: A model is only as trustworthy as its data, evaluation design, and production monitoring; the training API cannot compensate for biased or unrepresentative examples.
tip: Begin with a simple baseline and one business-relevant metric before experimenting with more complex trainers or AutoML.
warning: PredictionEngine is convenient for simple or single-threaded examples but is not thread-safe; production services should use an appropriate pooled or batch prediction pattern.
latestNote: New guide on classical machine learning and local inference

name: OpenAPI & Scalar
shortDescription: Generate accurate OpenAPI contracts and present an interactive, modern API reference with Scalar.
overview: ASP.NET Core can generate OpenAPI documents from endpoint metadata, while Scalar renders those documents as an interactive API reference for developers.
detail: Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi provides first-party document generation for Minimal APIs and controllers, including runtime endpoints, build-time generation, multiple documents, and transformers. Scalar.AspNetCore is a separate UI integration that reads the generated document and renders searchable reference documentation and a request client. Accurate endpoint metadata and deliberate document exposure matter more than the visual shell.

concepts.title: OpenAPI document
concepts.description: A language-neutral contract describing operations, paths, parameters, request bodies, responses, schemas, and security schemes.

concepts.title: Endpoint metadata
concepts.description: Typed results, attributes, summaries, descriptions, and response declarations feed the generated operation definitions.

concepts.title: Document transformers
concepts.description: Transformers apply cross-cutting changes such as security schemes, branding metadata, or environment-specific server information.

concepts.title: Scalar API reference
concepts.description: Scalar consumes an OpenAPI URL and provides interactive, searchable documentation without generating the contract itself.

architecture.description: ASP.NET Core endpoint metadata is assembled into an OpenAPI document, exposed as JSON, and consumed by Scalar or downstream client-generation tools.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: The app generates a first-party OpenAPI document and exposes Scalar only in development, while endpoint metadata improves the contract.

bestPractices: Treat the OpenAPI document as a tested contract and fail continuous integration when unintended breaking changes appear.
Use typed results and explicit metadata so status codes, schemas, descriptions, and security requirements match actual behavior.
Version APIs deliberately and publish separate documents when consumers need stable lifecycle boundaries.
Restrict or secure interactive documentation in production and never prefill real credentials or secrets in a browser-visible client.

interviewQuestions.question: What roles do Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi and Scalar play?
interviewQuestions.answer: The Microsoft package generates the OpenAPI document from ASP.NET Core metadata. Scalar consumes that document and renders an interactive reference; it does not replace accurate contract generation.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can generated documentation still be wrong?
interviewQuestions.answer: Generation reflects available metadata. If response types, status codes, security requirements, or descriptions are missing or differ from runtime behavior, the generated contract will preserve those gaps.

interviewQuestions.question: How should API versioning relate to OpenAPI documents?
interviewQuestions.answer: Each supported public API version should have a clear lifecycle and discoverable contract, commonly through separate named documents that client teams can pin and compare.

note: Scalar is a documentation experience; the OpenAPI document remains the portable source of truth for tools and consumers.
tip: Check the generated JSON into an artifact or compare it in CI so contract changes are reviewed alongside code.
warning: An unrestricted production documentation UI can expose internal operations and make credential misuse easier even when the underlying API still enforces authorization.
latestNote: New guide on first-party OpenAPI generation and Scalar

name: Feature Flags
shortDescription: Separate deployment from release with runtime flags, targeted rollouts, variants, and operational kill switches.
overview: Feature flags let teams change feature availability at runtime so code can be deployed independently from when or to whom a capability is released.
detail: Microsoft.FeatureManagement integrates flag evaluation with .NET configuration and dependency injection, while Azure App Configuration can centrally store and refresh definitions. Boolean flags support on or off decisions, filters enable time windows and targeting, and variants can assign different configurations to audiences. Flags reduce release risk only when ownership, observability, testing, and removal are treated as part of the feature lifecycle.

concepts.title: Deployment versus release
concepts.description: Code can reach production disabled, then be enabled gradually without building and deploying another artifact.

concepts.title: Feature filters
concepts.description: Time-window, percentage, targeting, and custom filters evaluate contextual rules instead of one global Boolean value.

concepts.title: Variants
concepts.description: A flag can assign named configurations to different audiences for experiments, migrations, or tier-specific behavior.

concepts.title: Flag lifecycle
concepts.description: Every flag needs an owner, purpose, expiry condition, telemetry, and cleanup plan to prevent permanent branching complexity.

architecture.description: A central configuration source supplies flag definitions, the feature manager evaluates them against request context, and application code selects the enabled behavior while telemetry records the decision.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: The feature manager is registered once and evaluated at the decision point, allowing a new checkout to be released independently from deployment.

bestPractices: Give every flag a clear owner, creation date, expected removal date, and documented behavior for configuration failure.
Evaluate flags at stable decision points and avoid scattering the same flag through many layers of the codebase.
Test both enabled and disabled paths, then observe errors, latency, and business metrics while rollout changes.
Remove temporary flags and dead branches promptly after a rollout or migration completes.

interviewQuestions.question: How is a feature flag different from application configuration?
interviewQuestions.answer: Both may use configuration infrastructure, but a feature flag represents a managed release decision with targeting, variants, telemetry, ownership, and a lifecycle rather than a general application setting.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a kill switch?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is an operational flag designed to disable risky behavior quickly without redeploying, with a safe and well-tested fallback path.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the main long-term risk of feature flags?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stale flags leave permanent branches and multiply the states developers must understand and test, so cleanup discipline is essential.

note: Feature flags make releases reversible, but they also add runtime states that must be observable and tested.
tip: Start rollout with internal users or a small stable audience and expand only when technical and business metrics remain healthy.
warning: Do not use a feature flag as the only authorization check; release targeting and security policy solve different problems.
latestNote: New guide on safe runtime releases and targeted rollouts

name: Model Context Protocol
shortDescription: Expose tools, resources, and prompts to AI applications through a standard protocol and the official C# SDK.
overview: Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how AI applications discover and invoke external tools, read contextual resources, and use reusable prompts.
detail: The official C# SDK lets .NET applications act as MCP servers or clients. Servers publish capabilities such as tools, resources, and prompts over transports including standard input/output and HTTP, while clients negotiate capabilities and invoke them through a consistent protocol. MCP improves interoperability, but every exposed capability remains a security boundary that needs validation, authorization, consent, timeouts, and auditability.

concepts.title: Servers and clients
concepts.description: An MCP server publishes capabilities; an MCP client connects, negotiates supported features, and makes those capabilities available to an AI host.

concepts.title: Tools
concepts.description: Model-invocable operations have typed inputs and outputs and can perform actions such as querying an order or creating a support ticket.

concepts.title: Resources and prompts
concepts.description: Resources expose contextual data through URIs, while prompts provide reusable, parameterized interaction templates.

concepts.title: Transports and lifecycle
concepts.description: Stdio suits local process integration, while HTTP supports remote services; initialization, capability negotiation, cancellation, and errors are protocol concerns.

architecture.description: An AI host uses an MCP client to discover server capabilities, then invokes narrowly scoped tools or reads resources through a negotiated transport.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: A small stdio server registers attributed tools from the assembly so compatible clients can discover and call the order-status capability.

bestPractices: Expose small, intention-revealing tools with strict schemas instead of giving a model generic database, shell, or network access.
Authenticate clients, authorize every capability and target resource, and require confirmation for destructive or financially meaningful actions.
Validate inputs and outputs, apply cancellation and timeouts, and return structured errors that do not reveal secrets or internal topology.
Log capability identity, caller, result, latency, and correlation data while redacting prompts, credentials, and sensitive payloads.

interviewQuestions.question: How is MCP different from function calling?
interviewQuestions.answer: Function calling is usually a model-provider feature for requesting a named function. MCP standardizes discovery, schemas, invocation, resources, prompts, transports, and lifecycle between AI hosts and external capability servers.

interviewQuestions.question: When should an MCP server use stdio instead of HTTP?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stdio is a good fit when the host starts and owns a local child process. HTTP is appropriate for independently deployed or remotely shared servers that need network authentication, scaling, and operations.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the main security risk of MCP tools?
interviewQuestions.answer: A model can turn untrusted instructions into real side effects. Tools must enforce the same authentication, authorization, validation, least privilege, and confirmation rules as any other application endpoint.

note: MCP standardizes integration mechanics; it does not decide whether a tool call is safe, permitted, or correct for a particular user.
tip: Start with one read-only tool and test discovery, schema clarity, cancellations, and audit logs before exposing write operations.
warning: Never expose an unrestricted shell, SQL executor, or broad cloud credential as an MCP tool.
latestNote: New guide on MCP servers, clients, tools, resources, and security

name: API Security & OWASP
shortDescription: Design and test ASP.NET Core APIs against common authorization, resource-consumption, configuration, and integration risks.
overview: API security applies identity, authorization, input boundaries, abuse controls, secure configuration, and continuous verification to every exposed operation and object.
detail: The OWASP API Security Top 10 highlights recurring risks including broken object-level authorization, broken authentication, unrestricted resource consumption, sensitive business-flow abuse, server-side request forgery, security misconfiguration, poor API inventory, and unsafe consumption of upstream APIs. ASP.NET Core supplies useful controls, but secure design begins with explicit assets, actors, trust boundaries, deny-by-default policy, and negative tests.

concepts.title: Object-level authorization
concepts.description: Every request for a specific record must verify the caller can access that object; a valid token alone does not prevent identifier-based data exposure.

concepts.title: Abuse and resource controls
concepts.description: Rate limits, request-size limits, pagination, timeouts, quotas, and workflow-specific rules protect compute and sensitive business flows.

concepts.title: Input and output boundaries
concepts.description: Purpose-built request and response models, validation, allowlists, and minimal serialization reduce mass assignment and excessive data exposure.

concepts.title: Inventory and dependencies
concepts.description: Teams must know which API versions and hosts exist, patch them, retire stale endpoints, and treat upstream API responses as untrusted input.

architecture.description: Traffic passes through edge protections and ASP.NET Core security controls before resource-aware authorization permits application logic to access protected data and dependencies.

code.label: OrderEndpoints.cs
code.introduction: The endpoint requires authentication and rate limiting, loads the target resource, then performs resource-aware authorization before returning a minimal response.

bestPractices: Threat-model APIs by asset, actor, trust boundary, and abuse case, then turn the findings into authorization and negative-test requirements.
Authorize the requested resource and tenant on the server for every operation; never trust a client-supplied owner, role, price, or workflow state.
Bound request size, query complexity, page size, concurrency, duration, and outbound destinations instead of relying on one global rate limit.
Maintain an API inventory, remove obsolete versions, patch dependencies, scan configuration, and test security controls in the deployed environment.

interviewQuestions.question: What is broken object-level authorization (BOLA)?
interviewQuestions.answer: It occurs when an API accepts an object identifier but does not verify that the authenticated caller is allowed to act on that specific object, allowing access by changing identifiers.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is rate limiting not a complete authorization control?
interviewQuestions.answer: Rate limiting controls volume, not permission. A caller below the limit can still access the wrong tenant, object, function, or business workflow unless authorization is enforced separately.

interviewQuestions.question: How should an API consume an upstream API safely?
interviewQuestions.answer: Authenticate the dependency, restrict destinations, set timeouts and size limits, validate responses, avoid blindly following redirects, and treat returned data as untrusted.

note: The OWASP list is an awareness and prioritization aid, not a substitute for a system-specific threat model.
tip: For every happy-path integration test, add anonymous, wrong-tenant, wrong-owner, oversized-input, and repeated-request cases.
warning: A globally authenticated API can still be critically vulnerable when object and function authorization are missing.
latestNote: New guide aligned with the OWASP API Security Top 10

name: Azure Key Vault & Secrets
shortDescription: Protect application secrets, keys, and certificates with managed identity, Azure RBAC, rotation, and auditable access.
overview: Azure Key Vault centralizes secrets, cryptographic keys, and certificates while Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC control who or what can use them.
detail: A .NET application can load Key Vault secrets through the ASP.NET Core configuration provider or use Azure SDK clients for explicit operations. DefaultAzureCredential supports developer identity locally and managed identity in Azure, avoiding deployed client secrets. Production design must also cover least-privilege data-plane roles, network access, rotation, caching, version behavior, diagnostics, recovery, and separation between environments.

concepts.title: Vault object types
concepts.description: Secrets hold sensitive values, keys support cryptographic operations, and certificates manage certificate material and lifecycle.

concepts.title: Managed identity
concepts.description: An Azure-hosted workload obtains short-lived Entra tokens without storing a client secret in source code or application configuration.

concepts.title: Azure RBAC
concepts.description: Separate control-plane and data-plane roles grant narrowly scoped management or object access and can be audited centrally.

concepts.title: Versions and rotation
concepts.description: Updating a secret creates a version; applications need an intentional refresh, rollout, fallback, and rollback strategy.

architecture.description: The .NET workload uses its Entra identity to request narrowly authorized Key Vault data, while diagnostics and rotation processes govern access throughout the secret lifecycle.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: The application adds Key Vault as a configuration source and uses the same credential chain for local development and managed identity in Azure.

bestPractices: Use managed identity for Azure workloads and developer identity or approved local secret storage during development; never commit credentials.
Prefer Azure RBAC data-plane roles, least privilege, separate vaults or strong boundaries per environment, and just-in-time administration.
Design secret rotation with overlapping validity, refresh behavior, observability, rollback, and dependency coordination before an emergency.
Enable diagnostics and alerts, protect recovery settings, restrict network access where appropriate, and avoid logging resolved secret values.

interviewQuestions.question: Why use managed identity with Key Vault?
interviewQuestions.answer: It removes the need to distribute and rotate an application credential for accessing the vault; Azure issues short-lived tokens to the workload identity.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the Key Vault control plane and data plane?
interviewQuestions.answer: The control plane manages the vault resource and settings, while the data plane operates on secrets, keys, and certificates. Permissions should be scoped separately.

interviewQuestions.question: Does rotating a Key Vault secret automatically update every running application?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. A new version becomes available, but each integration has its own caching and refresh behavior. Applications need a tested strategy for observing and adopting the new value.

note: Key Vault protects stored secret material, but callers can still leak a retrieved value through logs, exceptions, telemetry, or overly broad process access.
tip: Test rotation in a non-production environment using two valid credential versions before relying on the process during an incident.
warning: Do not replace one embedded application secret with another embedded credential used to access the vault.
latestNote: New guide on managed identity, RBAC, and secret rotation

name: Internal Developer Platforms
shortDescription: Create product-minded golden paths that give development teams secure, governed, observable self-service delivery.
overview: An internal developer platform (IDP) combines self-service workflows, reusable platform capabilities, and governance to reduce developer cognitive load from idea to production.
detail: Platform engineering treats developers as customers and the platform as a product. An IDP connects templates, source control, CI/CD, infrastructure, secrets, policy, observability, documentation, and service ownership into supported golden paths. For .NET teams, Aspire can standardize local orchestration, service discovery, health checks, telemetry, and deployment models, but it is one building block rather than the entire platform.

concepts.title: Golden paths
concepts.description: Recommended, supported routes encode proven defaults for common workloads while allowing documented escape hatches for genuine exceptions.

concepts.title: Self-service interfaces
concepts.description: Portals, CLIs, APIs, templates, and automation let teams provision and operate services without ticket-driven handoffs.

concepts.title: Platform as a product
concepts.description: A platform team researches developer needs, owns a roadmap and support model, and measures adoption and outcomes rather than mandating tools.

concepts.title: Governance by design
concepts.description: Security, cost, reliability, ownership, and compliance controls are built into reusable workflows with early feedback.

architecture.description: Developers use a portal, CLI, or template to invoke platform APIs that coordinate engineering systems and provision governed runtime capabilities with feedback and telemetry.

code.label: AppHost.cs
code.introduction: A reusable Aspire composition can form part of a .NET golden path by wiring dependencies, health, service discovery, and local orchestration consistently.

bestPractices: Start with a thin, high-friction developer journey and build the smallest viable golden path with teams that will use it.
Provide APIs, automation, documentation, support, and escape hatches; a catalog page alone is not a developer platform.
Encode secure defaults and policy feedback early, while keeping ownership boundaries and failure recovery visible to product teams.
Measure lead time, onboarding time, reliability, adoption, support load, and developer satisfaction instead of output such as template count.

interviewQuestions.question: How is an internal developer platform different from a developer portal?
interviewQuestions.answer: A portal is one possible user interface. An IDP includes the underlying APIs, automation, templates, policies, infrastructure capabilities, ownership model, and operational feedback.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a golden path?
interviewQuestions.answer: It is a supported route for a common workload that packages good defaults and automation to reduce cognitive load without forbidding justified alternatives.

interviewQuestions.question: Where does .NET Aspire fit in platform engineering?
interviewQuestions.answer: Aspire can standardize application composition, local dependencies, service discovery, health, telemetry, and deployment representations for .NET workloads, but CI/CD, cloud provisioning, policy, identity, catalogs, and product ownership still require a broader platform.

note: Successful platforms earn adoption by removing friction; they do not merely centralize control or rename an operations ticket queue.
tip: Interview developers and map one delivery journey before selecting portal or infrastructure products.
warning: A mandatory big-bang platform built without product-team feedback can increase cognitive load and create a new bottleneck.
latestNote: New guide on golden paths, self-service, governance, and Aspire

name: Dapper
shortDescription: Map parameterized SQL to .NET objects with a small, fast API built on standard ADO.NET connections.
overview: Dapper is a lightweight object mapper that extends ADO.NET database connections with APIs for executing parameterized SQL and mapping result rows to .NET types.
detail: Dapper deliberately leaves SQL, connections, transactions, schema evolution, and aggregate persistence decisions to the application. Query, Execute, QuerySingle, multi-mapping, multiple result sets, stored procedures, and asynchronous APIs cover common data-access needs with little abstraction. It is especially useful for explicit read models and performance-sensitive queries, and can coexist with EF Core when boundaries and transaction ownership are clear.

concepts.title: Explicit SQL
concepts.description: The application owns query text, joins, projections, indexes, and provider behavior rather than relying on a LINQ translator.

concepts.title: Parameter binding
concepts.description: Anonymous objects, POCOs, dictionaries, and DynamicParameters bind values safely and support input, output, and return parameters.

concepts.title: Row mapping
concepts.description: Column names map to typed objects, while multi-mapping and QueryMultiple handle joined objects and multiple result grids.

concepts.title: Transaction ownership
concepts.description: Dapper uses the supplied DbConnection and DbTransaction, so application code controls lifetime, atomicity, and coordination.

architecture.description: A query service owns explicit SQL and parameters, Dapper executes through an ADO.NET connection, and projected rows become focused read models.

code.label: OrderQueries.cs
code.introduction: A query object sends parameterized SQL through a provider connection and maps only the columns needed by the read model.

bestPractices: Always bind changing values as parameters; never concatenate user input, sort expressions, identifiers, or filter fragments into SQL.
Project only required columns, bound result sizes, inspect query plans, and add indexes based on measured production-shaped queries.
Open connections late, dispose them predictably, pass explicit transactions when operations must be atomic, and propagate cancellation.
Keep SQL and mapping tests close to the target database provider because syntax, types, casing, and query plans are provider-specific.

interviewQuestions.question: How is Dapper different from EF Core?
interviewQuestions.answer: Dapper maps explicit SQL over ADO.NET and provides little unit-of-work or change-tracking behavior. EF Core supplies LINQ translation, identity and change tracking, relationships, migrations, and a richer ORM model.

interviewQuestions.question: Can Dapper and EF Core be used together?
interviewQuestions.answer: Yes. A common CQRS approach uses EF Core for transactional writes and Dapper for explicit read projections, provided connection and transaction ownership are coordinated when atomicity is required.

interviewQuestions.question: Does using Dapper automatically prevent SQL injection?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Dapper makes parameter binding convenient, but dynamic SQL built by concatenating untrusted input is still vulnerable. Dynamic identifiers and sort choices require allowlists.

note: Dapper reduces mapping ceremony, not the need to understand SQL, transactions, indexes, connection pooling, and provider behavior.
tip: Use a dedicated read-model type whose property names intentionally match aliased result columns.
warning: A fast mapper cannot rescue an unbounded query, missing index, long transaction, or unsafe SQL construction.
latestNote: New guide on explicit SQL, mapping, transactions, and EF Core coexistence

name: Solution Architecture Fundamentals
shortDescription: Turn business outcomes and quality requirements into explicit system boundaries, views, tradeoffs, and evolutionary decisions.
overview: Solution architecture connects business goals, stakeholder concerns, quality requirements, and constraints to a coherent design that teams can build and operate.
detail: A solution architect clarifies the problem before selecting technology. The work includes identifying stakeholders and critical flows, expressing measurable quality attributes, defining system context and boundaries, comparing architecture styles, documenting significant decisions, designing for operations and security, and validating the architecture through prototypes, reviews, tests, and production evidence. Diagrams are communication tools; the architecture is the set of decisions and constraints that shape the system throughout its life.

concepts.title: Drivers and constraints
concepts.description: Business outcomes, critical user journeys, compliance, budget, schedule, existing systems, and team capabilities define the feasible design space.

concepts.title: Quality attributes
concepts.description: Reliability, security, performance, operability, cost, and maintainability become measurable scenarios rather than vague goals.

concepts.title: Boundaries and views
concepts.description: Context, container, component, deployment, data, and runtime views explain different stakeholder concerns without one overloaded diagram.

concepts.title: Tradeoffs and evolution
concepts.description: Styles and technologies are selected against requirements, recorded as decisions, validated early, and revisited as evidence or constraints change.

architecture.description: Stakeholder outcomes and constraints shape measurable requirements, which guide architecture decisions and views that delivery teams validate through implementation and operations.

code.label: QualityScenario.cs
code.introduction: A small quality-scenario record forces an architecture requirement to name its stimulus, operating condition, expected response, and measurable target.

bestPractices: Start with business outcomes, stakeholders, critical flows, constraints, and measurable quality scenarios before choosing services or patterns.
Use a small set of complementary views and keep every diagram scoped, labeled, versioned, and connected to decisions.
Evaluate options against explicit criteria, record material tradeoffs, and prototype the assumptions with the highest cost of being wrong.
Include deployment, observability, security, data ownership, failure recovery, cost, and team ownership in the architecture from the start.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between architecture and design?
interviewQuestions.answer: Architecture focuses on system-shaping structures, constraints, quality attributes, and costly-to-reverse decisions. Design also includes the many local implementation choices made within those boundaries.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you choose an architecture style?
interviewQuestions.answer: Compare styles against business drivers, quality scenarios, constraints, operational model, data needs, team capabilities, and migration path; then validate the riskiest assumptions.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you know an architecture is working?
interviewQuestions.answer: Define measurable fitness criteria for critical qualities, test them before release, observe them in production, review incidents and costs, and change decisions when evidence no longer supports them.

note: Architecture documentation should make important reasoning discoverable, not attempt to predict every implementation detail.
tip: Write the three most important quality scenarios and use them as evaluation criteria in every architecture review.
warning: A polished diagram without measurable requirements, ownership, tradeoffs, or validation is not an executable architecture.
latestNote: New guide on requirements, views, tradeoffs, and architecture validation

name: Architecture Decision Records
shortDescription: Capture architecturally significant choices with their context, considered options, consequences, ownership, and lifecycle.
overview: An Architecture Decision Record documents why a significant design choice was made and what consequences the team accepts.
detail: An ADR is a short, version-controlled record for a decision that shapes structure, quality attributes, constraints, or future options. It captures the context and forces, the decision, alternatives considered, expected positive and negative consequences, status, owners, and links to evidence. ADRs form a chronological decision log: accepted decisions are not silently rewritten when direction changes; a new record supersedes the old one and preserves the reasoning available at the time.

concepts.title: Architectural significance
concepts.description: Record choices that affect system structure, key qualities, organizational boundaries, or options that are expensive to reverse.

concepts.title: Context and options
concepts.description: State the problem, drivers, constraints, assumptions, and credible alternatives so the decision can be understood independently.

concepts.title: Consequences
concepts.description: Document benefits, costs, risks, operational effects, follow-up work, and the conditions that would trigger reconsideration.

concepts.title: Decision lifecycle
concepts.description: Use proposed, accepted, rejected, deprecated, and superseded states with owners, dates, and links to later decisions.

architecture.description: A significant concern is evaluated against drivers and options, accepted through review, and preserved in a versioned decision log that informs delivery and later reassessment.

code.label: docs/adr/0007-api-gateway.md
code.introduction: A compact template keeps records comparable while leaving room for evidence and explicit tradeoffs.
code.code:
# ADR-0007: Use a managed API gateway

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-08-06
- Owners: Platform Architecture

## Context
Public APIs need consistent authentication, quotas, version routing,
and telemetry across independently deployed services.

## Decision
Use Azure API Management as the external gateway.

## Alternatives
- Application-owned gateway
- Direct exposure through an ingress controller

## Consequences
Central policy and analytics improve consistency, but APIM adds cost,
latency, operational dependencies, and tier-specific constraints.

## Revisit when
Traffic, regions, or gateway availability targets materially change.

bestPractices: Keep ADRs concise, immutable after acceptance except for status and links, and store them beside the code or architecture documentation they govern.
Record only significant decisions and state the context, options, decision, consequences, owners, date, and review trigger.
Use lightweight peer review and include links to prototypes, measurements, threat models, cost estimates, and diagrams that support the choice.
Supersede an obsolete ADR with a new record instead of erasing history, and review the decision log during major changes and incidents.

interviewQuestions.question: Which decisions deserve an ADR?
interviewQuestions.answer: Decisions that materially shape the system, affect important quality attributes or organizational boundaries, impose constraints, or are difficult and expensive to reverse.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should an accepted ADR not simply be edited?
interviewQuestions.answer: Editing destroys the historical reasoning and makes it unclear what teams implemented. A superseding ADR preserves chronology while documenting the new context and decision.

interviewQuestions.question: How do ADRs avoid becoming bureaucracy?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use a short template, record only significant choices, keep review close to normal code workflows, assign ownership, and link each record to delivery or validation evidence.

note: An ADR explains a decision; it does not replace diagrams, API contracts, threat models, runbooks, or implementation documentation.
tip: Start a brownfield decision log by reconstructing only the few choices currently constraining change, then record new decisions as they occur.
warning: A decision log that records only the selected option and omits context, alternatives, and consequences cannot support future reassessment.
latestNote: New guide on concise, versioned architecture decisions

name: API Design Best Practices
shortDescription: Design stable, secure, observable HTTP contracts around resources, standard semantics, compatibility, and predictable failure behavior.
overview: Good API design creates a clear, loosely coupled contract that clients can use correctly and evolve with safely.
detail: An HTTP API should model business resources and workflows rather than database tables or implementation methods. Consistent URIs, HTTP methods, status codes, media types, validation errors, pagination, filtering, concurrency controls, idempotency, asynchronous operations, versioning, security, and observability make behavior predictable. Contract-first review and compatibility tests help providers and consumers evolve independently while explicit deprecation policies prevent permanent support for accidental behavior.

concepts.title: Resource-oriented contracts
concepts.description: Stable nouns, representations, relationships, and workflow resources describe the domain without exposing internal storage or service boundaries.

concepts.title: HTTP semantics
concepts.description: Methods, safety, idempotency, status codes, headers, caching, conditional requests, and content negotiation communicate standard behavior.

concepts.title: Scale and resilience
concepts.description: Pagination, filtering, field selection, rate limits, timeouts, idempotency keys, and asynchronous operations bound work and support retries.

concepts.title: Evolution and governance
concepts.description: OpenAPI review, compatibility checks, explicit versioning, deprecation windows, security defaults, and telemetry protect clients over time.

architecture.description: Clients use a versioned contract through security and policy controls; resource handlers enforce domain rules while telemetry and compatibility checks govern evolution.

code.label: Program.cs
code.introduction: A resource endpoint uses a constrained route, typed outcomes, cancellation, and a standard validation problem response.

bestPractices: Design from consumer workflows and domain resources, publish an OpenAPI contract, and review it before implementation.
Apply standard HTTP semantics consistently, return Problem Details for machine-readable errors, and document every status and retry behavior.
Bound collections and work with pagination, filters, payload limits, quotas, timeouts, cancellation, and asynchronous patterns for long operations.
Define compatibility, versioning, deprecation, security, idempotency, concurrency, and observability policies as part of the contract.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes an HTTP operation idempotent?
interviewQuestions.answer: Repeating the same request has the same intended effect on server state as making it once. GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, and safe retry mechanisms should respect that property even if response codes differ.

interviewQuestions.question: When should an API return 202 Accepted?
interviewQuestions.answer: When work has been accepted but will complete asynchronously. The response should identify a status resource or operation URL and document polling, completion, failure, and cancellation behavior.

interviewQuestions.question: How can an API evolve without breaking clients?
interviewQuestions.answer: Prefer additive changes, tolerant readers, contract compatibility tests, explicit policies for breaking versions, usage telemetry, and a communicated deprecation window.

note: REST is one useful interaction style, not a requirement for every internal or event-driven interface; choose the style from consumer and system needs.
tip: Review a proposed API using only its OpenAPI document and example errors; hidden assumptions discovered there are cheaper to fix than deployed contracts.
warning: Exposing database tables directly couples clients to internal storage, expands the attack surface, and makes later redesign unnecessarily breaking.
latestNote: New guide on HTTP contracts, evolution, reliability, and governance

name: Multi-Tenancy Patterns
shortDescription: Balance tenant isolation, scale, cost, customization, and operations across identity, compute, data, messaging, and deployment.
overview: Multitenant architecture serves multiple customers from a solution while deliberately controlling isolation, scale, cost, performance, and customization.
detail: Multitenancy is not one binary infrastructure choice. Each component can be pooled, partitioned, stamped, or dedicated according to data sensitivity, performance, geography, commercial tier, and operational requirements. Tenant identity must be derived from trusted authentication context and enforced through every data and cache path. A control plane automates onboarding, placement, configuration, lifecycle, and metering while quotas, partitioning, observability, and tests protect tenants from leakage and noisy neighbors.

concepts.title: Isolation models
